findings.at: packages/modern-cmdk-codemod/src/transforms/should-filter.ts:33-36 at 640f4ce (the header paragraph on the adapter's 0-to-false mapping)
findings.groupTitle: The should-filter header says the core reads a score of 0 as a score; since ARCH-14 a score of 0 or less excludes the item
findings.claim: should-filter.ts:33-36 says modern-cmdk 'reads `false` as "exclude" and any number, 0 included, as a score (core/machine.ts:66-80)', so the adapter maps 0 to false. Since 5393621 (ARCH-14, 1.6.0) the custom-filter adapter in core/machine.ts excludes an item whose filter returns 0 or a negative number, as it does for false; the cited line range is also stale. The mapping the adapter writes is now redundant on a 1.6.0 core and still correct output.
findings.fix: Rewrite the paragraph: the core (1.6.0, ARCH-14) excludes false, 0 and negative scores, so the adapter's 0-to-false mapping is kept for migrated code that still runs on a 1.5.x core and is a no-op on 1.6.0; cite the machine.ts custom-filter adapter by its current line range. No behaviour change; the codemod snapshot tests stay as they are.
findings.note: The should-filter header now says the 1.6.0 core excludes false, 0 and negative scores (ARCH-14; cites the custom-filter adapter at core/machine.ts:73-87), so the adapter's 0-to-false mapping stays for output that runs on a 1.5.x core and is a no-op on 1.6.0. Comment only; the codemod tests are unchanged.

findings.groupTitle: SearchEngine.index() is documented as 'call on registration' but UPDATE_ITEM re-indexes through it and an indexed id is replaced
findings.claim: The JSDoc at search/types.ts:19 reads 'Index items for fast lookup (call on registration)'. Since aca8737 (ARCH-20) the machine also calls searchEngine.index([event.item]) on UPDATE_ITEM (machine.ts:328), and the default engine's index() sets indexedEntries by id (search/index.ts:64), so an id already indexed is replaced by the new item. The interface contract a pluggable engine must honour (replace on re-index) is unstated, and the parenthesis is incomplete.
findings.fix: Rewrite the JSDoc: 'Indexes items for lookup. Called on registration and again on UPDATE_ITEM; an id that is already indexed is replaced by the new item, so a pluggable engine must overwrite, not append.' Check the WASM and worker engines honour it (their index() must replace too) and say so in the comment of each; a unit test on the default engine (index twice, search, the new value wins) pins it.
findings.note: SearchEngine.index JSDoc (search/types.ts) states the contract: called on registration and again on UPDATE_ITEM, an id already indexed is replaced, and (96f7313) indexing is incremental: ids not in the call stay indexed. Test tests/unit/search.test.ts 'CE-106: indexing an id again replaces the item' (green on the default engine, which upserts by id). The WASM and worker engines do not honour it (index() replaces the whole item list): that is W04, W44 and ARCH-05 (1.9.0 / 1.11.0), unchanged here; no comment claims otherwise.

findings.at: packages/modern-cmdk/src/core/machine.ts, the batching block (queued, nextQueued, inHandler, dirty, changed) and [Symbol.dispose] at 640f4ce
findings.groupTitle: A handler that disposes the machine mid-batch and then reuses it leaves the batch counter negative, so that machine never emits again
findings.claim: [Symbol.dispose] resets queued and nextQueued to 0 (c339027, so a disposed machine that is used again still batches). If a listener disposes the machine from inside a batch handler and the same machine is then sent events again, the handlers still running decrement queued past the reset and it goes negative; commit() runs only when queued reaches 0, so the reused machine never emits again. Reachable only by dispose-in-handler followed by reuse; reported by the CORE/machine cluster on 2026-11-08, not reproduced in a test yet.
findings.fix: Clamp the decrement (queued = Math.max(0, queued - 1)) or, with RA-03 and CE-78 (re-create the machine after dispose in use-command-setup.ts), make a disposed machine refuse further sends so reuse is impossible; test: a listener that disposes inside a batch, then send again, assert one stateChange.

findings.groupTitle: An UPDATE_ITEM on the earlier item of a shared shortcut re-binds it to the top of the stack, so a label-only update changes which item the key fires
findings.claim: Since 02d6823 a key holds a binding stack and the first registration wins (CE-08, DAE-32). bind() in machine.ts unbinds the item's old binding and registers again on REGISTER_ITEM and UPDATE_ITEM, so any UPDATE_ITEM on the earlier of two items sharing a key (in React: a change to its value, keywords, shortcut, disabled or groupId) pushes it to the top of the stack and it wins again. The hostile verifier of the fix round measured it on 2026-11-08: a label-only update to item a made a win over b on the before and after builds of c5f224d. The conflict report is unchanged; only the winner moves.
findings.fix: When bind() re-registers an item on a key it already holds, replace its binding in place (same stack position, new handler and item) instead of unregister-then-register; a changed key still unregisters the old one (CE-49). Test in tests/unit/machine.test.ts: a then b on one key, UPDATE_ITEM a's label, press the key, b's onSelect fires; red on the current code.
findings.note: register() already replaced an item's own binding on the same key in place; the defect was bind() in machine.ts calling unregisterByItem first on every REGISTER_ITEM/UPDATE_ITEM, which moved the item to the top of the stack. unregisterByItem(itemId, keep?) now spares the kept key, so bind() drops only the item's bindings on other keys (CE-49 stays green), and under shortcutAction 'direct' an item without onSelect keeps no old binding. Tests tests/unit/shortcut-rebind.test.ts: 'CE-108: UPDATE_ITEM of the earlier binding on a shared key leaves the later binding winning' (red before: a fired), 'CE-108: UPDATE_ITEM swaps the handler of the binding in place', 'CE-108: a changed key still drops the old key and joins the new key on top', 'CE-108: register() for an item already bound on that key replaces the binding in place', 'CE-108: unregisterByItem(item, keep) drops the item on every key but the kept one'. +13 B core.

findings.groupTitle: Frecency hydration at an empty query, or an empty load, emits one stateChange with unchanged filteredIds and re-renders every frecency palette once after mount
findings.claim: 640f4ce (CE-14) marks the results dirty and commits when the frecency load settles. Frecency re-ranks only non-empty queries (DT-18 ruling, 863eb8a) and a filter of false lists every item in registration order, so at an empty query or with filter: false the hydration refilter produces the same filteredIds and the emitted stateChange is redundant; every React palette with frecency re-renders once after mount for nothing. Also with an empty storage (nothing loaded). Found by the hostile verifier of the rebased commit on 2026-11-08.
findings.fix: Return early in the load callback when disposed, state.search === '' or options.filter === false (the engine has merged the records; the next non-empty query ranks with them), plus a test 'hydration at an empty query emits no stateChange' and one that a non-empty query at hydration still re-ranks (CE-14 stays green).
findings.note: The frecency load callback returns early when disposed, when the query is empty or when filter is false (frecency re-ranks only non-empty queries, DT-18; filter false lists registration order), so a frecency palette no longer re-renders once after mount for an unchanged list. Test tests/unit/frecency-machine.test.ts 'CE-109: hydration at an empty query emits no stateChange' (red before: 1 of 11) and (96f7313) 'CE-109: hydration under filter: false emits no stateChange and keeps registration order' (red with the filter clause removed: 1 of 12); 'CE-14: hydration re-ranks the current results without another event' stays green; a queued SEARCH_CHANGE at load settle still ranks with the records. The comment above the block states the rule. +11 B core.

findings.groupTitle: A commit() that throws inside the hydration callback surfaces as an unhandled rejection, while the same throw from a batch surfaces as an uncaught exception
findings.claim: The hydration refilter runs inside the load promise's .then(); if commit() throws there (a search engine or a stateChange listener throwing), the error becomes an unhandled rejection of a promise nobody holds, whereas the same listener throwing from a send() batch is rethrown by the scheduler as an uncaught exception. Both are visible; the channel differs, so a host's error handler sees two shapes for one defect. Found by the hostile verifier of 640f4ce on 2026-11-08.
findings.fix: Rethrow from the callback through queueMicrotask(() => { throw error }) (or run the hydration commit through the scheduler) so both paths surface as uncaught exceptions; test with a throwing listener installed before the load settles.

findings.at: packages/modern-cmdk/src/core/frecency/index.ts:169-172 at 640f4ce (the dirty flag is cleared before the queued save runs)
findings.groupTitle: A timer save that rejects leaves the engine clean, so a later asyncDispose resolves without retrying and the data is only warned about
findings.claim: flush() clears the dirty flag before the save runs (e8c042e). If the save a timer started rejects, the engine is already clean: a later [Symbol.asyncDispose] finds nothing to save and resolves, the failure is reported once through console.warn and the selections are lost; the sync dispose path retries once and warns. Pre-existing before the 1.6.0 frecency branch (the flag was cleared the same way); reported by the CORE/frecency manager on 2026-11-08 as an unfixed minor gap.
findings.fix: Decide dirtiness inside the queued chain: clear the flag only when the save resolved, set it again when it rejected (keeping the one-warning rule), so asyncDispose retries once; test: a storage whose first save rejects and second resolves, asyncDispose persists the records.

findings.at: packages/modern-cmdk/src/core/frecency/idb-storage.ts, the store creation path added by b292896 (SEC-35) at 640f4ce
findings.groupTitle: Three or more IdbFrecencyStorage store names opening one database at the same moment can hit a VersionError that nothing handles
findings.claim: b292896 fixed SEC-35 (a second storeName in an existing database) by upgrading the database version to add the object store. Two stores opening at once are serialised by the upgrade path; with three or more store names opening the same database in the same moment, an open whose requested version is already below the one another upgrade just set gets a VersionError, which is neither retried nor reported. Reported by the CORE/frecency manager on 2026-11-08 as unhandled; not reproduced in a test.
findings.fix: Retry an open that fails with VersionError once with the current version (or route store creation through one shared upgrade promise per database name); test three storages on one database name opened in one tick, all save and load.

findings.at: apps/playground/src/styles.css:499-502 and :761 at 640f4ce (the playground's disabled-item opacity and forced-colors rules)
findings.groupTitle: The playground's own opacity: 0.6 on disabled items overrides the library's forced-colors opacity: 1, so the High Contrast demo does not show the library's rule
findings.claim: react/styles.css:580-583 sets opacity: 1 on a disabled item under forced-colors (GrayText carries the state). apps/playground/src/styles.css:499-502 sets opacity: 0.6 on the same element with higher specificity, and :761 sets GrayText itself, so in the High Contrast demo the library's forced-colors rule is not what the user sees and the PGX-13 e2e colour assertion (c27c040) passes on the playground's rule, not the library's. Reported by the CORE/machine cluster on 2026-11-08.
findings.fix: Scope the playground's disabled opacity out of forced-colors (`@media (forced-colors: none)`) and drop its own GrayText at :761 so the library rule paints the demo; keep the PGX-13 assertion, which then isolates the library; the docs render test of the High Contrast page stays green.
findings.note: The playground's disabled opacity, its disabled colour and the base item colour moved under `@media (forced-colors: none)` and its own GrayText is gone, so the library's forced-colors rule (react/styles.css:580-583) paints the High Contrast demo; scoping only the opacity left the item black because the playground's later-layer colour beat the library's GrayText (seen in Chromium). The PGX-13 e2e test gained toHaveCSS('opacity', '1'): 1 failed → 2 passed under `--project=chromium -g forced-colors`; verifier mutations of the library rule (both declarations, opacity only, colour only) and of the playground scoping all red; a colour probe shows every other item state unchanged in both modes. Compat source: @mdn/browser-compat-data 8.1.8: forced-colors Safari 16 / Firefox 89, CSS nesting Safari 17.2 / Firefox 117 (read 2026-11-08). Chromium is the gate (D85); Safari has no forced-colors mode; Firefox not observed.

findings.groupTitle: No accuracy case has competing matches, so a reversed sort passes every expectedTopResult assertion
findings.claim: PERF-13 (1a6c208) names the expected top result for gtdf, gc and tsd, but each of those queries matches exactly one corpus entry, so the assertion proves recall, not ranking: the CORE/tests cluster measured a reversed sort staying 75 of 75 green on 2026-11-08. Only the exact and multi-word cases rank among competitors.
findings.fix: Add a case whose query matches several corpus entries with distinct scores (for example a prefix shared by three commands where one is an exact word match) and assert the order of the top two; do it with the T18 redesign (test.for cases with real thresholds) in 1.9.0.

findings.at: scripts/consumer-smoke.ts:65 at 835b29c (CORE_COPY_LITERAL = '[modern-cmdk] FrecencyEngine dispose flush failed:')
findings.groupTitle: The consumer smoke test counts core copies by a FrecencyEngine warning string that the frecency landing renamed, so every consumer job reported 0 copies and CI went red
findings.claim: scripts/consumer-smoke.ts counts how many copies of the core a consumer's client bundle holds by counting CORE_COPY_LITERAL, the FrecencyEngine warning '[modern-cmdk] FrecencyEngine dispose flush failed:'. e8c042e (CE-01/SEC-02) rewrote the engine's warnings ('[modern-cmdk] save failed:'), so the literal no longer exists in dist/core/index.mjs; on 835b29c the three consumer jobs of CI run 42449432890 reported 'core copies 0, expected 1' for vite, next-webpack and next-turbopack while every other job passed. Nothing in the unit suite pinned the literal to the source, so the rename passed the local gate and the pre-push gate and failed only on GitHub.
findings.fix: Point CORE_COPY_LITERAL at a warning the core entry always carries ('[modern-cmdk] frecency load failed:' in core/machine.ts, present once in dist/core/index.mjs) and add a unit test to tests/unit/consumer-smoke.test.ts that reads packages/modern-cmdk/src and asserts the literal occurs exactly once there, so a future rename fails at `pnpm test` (and in the pre-push gate) before the consumer jobs. Document the coupling beside the constant.
findings.note: Fixed the same hour: CI run 42449432890 on 835b29c went red in the three consumer jobs only; the marker moved to the machine's frecency-load warning and the unit test pins it to src (red with the old literal: 1 failed; green after). The next release/1.6.0 CI run is the proof.

findings.groupTitle: send() has no disposed guard: after dispose an event is still applied and the options callbacks fire
findings.claim: machine.send() checks nothing about disposal: after dispose() an OPEN event is still reduced into state and the options callbacks (onOpenChange, onSelect, onSearchChange) still fire; only the subscribe listeners stay silent because dispose cleared them (the TUB-36 test asserts exactly that and no more). Found by the wave B manager while writing the TUB-36 test.
findings.fix: `if (disposed) return;` at the top of send() (and of flush paths that reach the reducer), with a machine-integration test: after dispose, OPEN leaves state.open false and onOpenChange uncalled, SEARCH_CHANGE leaves onSearchChange uncalled, ITEM_SELECT leaves onSelect uncalled.
findings.note: Held back from 1.6.0 on 2026-11-08: `if (disposed) return;` in send() turns two pinned behaviours red: tests/unit/machine.test.ts:569 'batching: events dropped by dispose do not stall the batches of a machine that is used again' sends REGISTER_ITEM after dispose on purpose, and tests/unit/command.test.tsx:255 'StrictMode: the machine keeps registering items and filtering' relies on it: use-command-setup.ts disposes the machine on the StrictMode unmount and the remount re-runs only the effect, so the children keep the machine captured at render, which is the disposed one. Reuse after dispose is therefore a deliberate 1.x behaviour until the adapter's StrictMode handling changes (CE-78 / RA-03, 1.7.0); the guard lands with them. dispose() already cancels the pending scheduler batch (scheduler[Symbol.dispose]() drops pending work), so a batch pending at dispose never runs; only a handler that disposes mid-batch lets the batch's remaining events through. Patch kept at R/ce113-guard-and-t11.patch (+10 B core).

findings.groupTitle: bench:compare fails the Benchmarks job on a single harness run against a baseline from another Node nightly: runner noise tripped the 15 % threshold with no code regression
findings.claim: CI run 42452131225 on release/1.6.0 ca9ae6f failed the Benchmarks job at `pnpm bench:compare` (exit 2): search:ts-scorer-10k 3.462 → 4.019 ms (+16.1 %) and stateUpdate:searchChange 0.368 → 0.438 ms (+19.0 %) against benchmarks/baseline.json, which was recorded on an AMD EPYC 7763 runner under Node v28.0.0-nightly20261103 while the job ran nightly 20261107. An A/B on the development host (worktrees ff2745c vs ca9ae6f, five alternating harness runs each) measured the head at −2.4 % and −3.8 % on the same two tasks with a base spread of 5 % and 11 %, so no commit landed since the green run on ff2745c explains the swing; stateUpdate:navigate moved +51 % on a 0.5 µs figure in the same job. The gate takes the mean of three runs' p50 and fails on one comparison, so runner and Node-nightly variance of this size turns the job red.
findings.fix: D93: compare-baseline.ts takes the median of five runs' p50 (p99 and rme likewise); the CI step re-runs the comparison once on exit 2 and is red only when both runs fail, surfacing the first failure as a warning; CONTRIBUTING states the rule; benchmarks/baseline.json is re-recorded from the benchmark-results artifact of the first green run after each Node pin bump (the orchestrator, at the RC and at each sweep that moves Node). Thresholds (5 % warn, 15 % fail) and the floor unchanged.
findings.note: CI run 42460937098 (201f701, the first fully green run of release/1.6.0): the Benchmarks job green under D93 (median of five, retry once) on the first push after the landing.

findings.groupTitle: The browser-bench CI job (10K mount gate, Chromium) has not run on GitHub yet
findings.claim: 1.6/bench adds the job 'Browser bench (Chromium, 10K mount gate)' (id browser-bench, needs build, artifact browser-bench-results; the CI Summary needs 19 jobs) with a 50 ms limit on the 10K mount median. It has only run on the development host (18.80 ms at f5fcebb, Intel Core Ultra 9 290HX). Per SEC-72 a CI job counts as working only once it is green on GitHub; the roadmap's 1.6.0 exit gate ('10K mount <= 50 ms on the CI image per the bench', G12, D81) depends on it.
findings.fix: Lands with 1.6/bench; closes when a CI run of release/1.6.0 shows the job green (run id recorded on the row). If the ubuntu runner misses 50 ms, the limit is re-set from the runner's measurement by an orchestrator ruling, never silently.
findings.note: CI run 42460937098 (201f701, the first fully green run of release/1.6.0): the browser-bench job's first GitHub run green (10K mount median on the ubuntu-26.04 runner recorded here).

findings.groupTitle: MEM-3 asserts that 10K unsubscribed listeners are released after one garbage-collection pass; one WeakRef of 10000 survived a pass on the react-floor CI lane
findings.claim: CI run 42455685144 (release/1.6.0 at 8362840) failed only in the job 'React react-floor' at tests/unit/memory-leak.test.ts:133: `expected [ WeakRef{} ] to have a length of +0 but got 1` after `await collectGarbage()`. Every other Test job of the same run (ubuntu-26.04, macos-26, windows-2025-vs2026 at Node 26.4.0 and the 28 nightly, and react-stable) passed the same test, as did the pre-push gate, so the single-pass collection is nondeterministic: 9999 of 10000 listeners were released, which is not a leak pattern. The test's claim (released, never fire) is right; its instrument (one collection) is not.
findings.fix: collectGarbage(settled?) loops major collections (gc with execution 'async' and the last-resort flavor where this Node's gc accepts options) with a macrotask turn between passes until the caller's predicate holds, bounded; every call site passes the predicate it then asserts; the assertions stay strict. Proven by 50 runs idle and under load with zero failures and by a scratch edit that keeps one listener referenced turning MEM-3 red.
findings.note: CI run 42460937098 (201f701): the React react-floor job, MEM-3 included, passed on the first run after the fix (60a9f96); the one-pass flake of run 42455685144 has not recurred.

findings.groupTitle: FrecencyEngine.load() is not chained into #pending, so a save that runs before the load resolves writes the new selection alone
findings.claim: core/frecency/index.ts:101-116 and :172 with core/machine.ts:102: load() merges into the engine's records when it resolves, but nothing a save waits on includes that load; with a storage whose load resolves late (a cold IndexedDB open, a slow custom storage), a selection's debounced save, flush() or dispose writes the engine's current records, which hold only the new selection, and the stored history is lost. Probed by the DOCS cluster's verifier with a delayed-load storage: the only save held only the new selection.
findings.fix: A save waits for the in-flight load, so the write holds the merged state (frequencies added, later lastUsed kept); flush() and dispose await it too; a rejected load does not block saves. Tests with a delayed-load storage and a rejecting load; mutation (unchained load) red.
findings.note: FrecencyEngine.load() sets a never-rejecting #loading promise (the merge moved to #merge()); every flush (the debounced save, the page-exit save, flush() and both disposals) awaits #pending and #loading before it saves, so a selection before the load settles writes the merged history once and a rejecting load releases the save. Three tests in tests/unit/frecency-engine.test.ts (delayed load: one merged write; flush and dispose wait for the load; a rejecting load releases the save); the unchained mutant turns all three red. D96 (940012b): a load that rejects sets #loadFailed and the flush path writes only while it is clear, so a history the engine could not read is never replaced; the rejecting-load test asserts flush() and asyncDispose() settle with no save; the flag mutant turns exactly that test red. A load that never settles holds every save and await using with it (documented in the load() and flush() JSDoc).

findings.groupTitle: Under React StrictMode the hook's cleanup disposes the frecencyStorage the caller passed in, so the re-mounted machine saves nothing
findings.claim: react/hooks/use-command-setup.ts:49-56: StrictMode's dev double-mount runs the effect cleanup, which disposes the machine, which disposes the FrecencyEngine, which disposes its storage; the effect re-runs and mounts a machine on the disposed storage, so `<Command frecency={{ enabled: true, storage: new IdbFrecencyStorage() }}>` persists nothing in development. Probed by the DOCS cluster's verifier with StrictMode and fake-indexeddb: 0 records with an inline storage, 1 record through a view object whose dispose is a no-op (the workaround guide/frecency.md and examples/frecency.md teach on 1.6/docs).
findings.fix: D95: ownership follows creation. A storage the caller passes (core option or React prop) is the caller's to dispose; the engine and the machine dispose only a storage they created. The React hook passes the caller's storage through unchanged. Tests: core (caller-passed storage survives machine dispose; a machine-created one is disposed) and React StrictMode (storage not disposed, one save). The frecency docs drop the view-object workaround afterwards.
findings.note: D95 (G-49): ownership follows creation. #ownsStorage is true only when no storage option was passed; #disposeStorage disposes only an owned storage (today the default MemoryFrecencyStorage); the JSDoc of FrecencyOptions.storage states the rule, and the React prop type extends CommandMachineOptions so it covers <Command frecency={{ storage }}> too; use-command-setup.ts passes the option through unchanged. Tests: frecency-engine.test.ts (a caller's storage survives both disposals; an engine-created one is disposed), frecency-machine.test.ts (P07 rewritten to the new contract, an owned-storage test, DG-63 disposes storage A itself) and the new tests/unit/frecency-strict-mode.test.tsx (StrictMode render, click, unmount: the spy storage is undisposed with exactly one save). The forced-dispose mutant turns four tests red. The frecency docs drop the view-object workaround in the follow-up commit. 8c683cf makes the use-command-setup.ts:50-51 comment true (the ref is nulled; the next root render creates a fresh machine; until then the subtree holds the disposed one: CE-124) and corrects two test comments (frecency-machine.test.ts:388, frecency-strict-mode.test.tsx:29).

findings.groupTitle: The WASM engine's index() replaces the whole index instead of adding to it, breaking the SearchEngine.index contract
findings.claim: core/search/wasm-engine.ts:48-57 with packages/command-search-wasm/crate/src/trigram.rs:30-31: each index(items) call rebuilds the trigram index from the items it is handed, while core/types.ts:24-27 defines index() as incremental (the machine indexes items as they register); through the machine only the last registered batch stays searchable. Read by the DOCS cluster's verifier and worker, not reproduced (the wasm build needs pkg/).
findings.fix: The crate's index adds to the existing index (or the TS adapter accumulates and re-indexes the whole set); a test through the machine registers items in two batches and searches across both. Filed for the next release that builds the wasm package in CI; not a published-package defect today (command-search-wasm is private).
findings.note: FIXED at 16d5a9b (1.7.0 C5, 1.7/c5): the main-thread wasm adapter keeps a Map<ItemId, string> of indexed items; index() upserts into it and remove() deletes only the given ids, so a second index() batch no longer replaces the first. The whole map goes to the crate once before the next search after a change (4f04f68: a rebuild per registration cost 73 s for 10K single REGISTER_ITEM events on the real build, 11 ms after; a payload the crate rejects keeps the engine stale so the next search throws again, 6277983). wasm-engine.real.test.ts runs against the built pkg/ (skipped without it unless MODERN_CMDK_REQUIRE_WASM_PKG=1, which the rust-wasm CI job sets). Closing test: 'CE-116: two index() batches through the machine are both searchable in the real wasm build' (real build) plus the mocked index-map tests. Opus-verifier, three rounds: mutations batch-only serialisation, clear-on-remove, no re-sync, filter removed, limit items.length, stale not set by index()/remove(), stale cleared before the crate call: each red on its test.

findings.groupTitle: onOpenChange fires on every OPEN/CLOSE, including at mount and on CLOSE while already closed, so a controlled dialog gets echo callbacks
findings.claim: react/dialog.tsx:69-73 with core/machine.ts:148-152: the machine emits openChange on every OPEN/CLOSE event whether or not the state changed, and the dialog forwards each to onOpenChange; a controlled dialog therefore receives a callback for its own prop change at mount and for a redundant CLOSE. Probed at the machine level by the DOCS cluster's verifier (CLOSE while closed emits openChange(false)); the React mount echo was read, not run.
findings.fix: openChange (and onOpenChange) fire only when `open` actually changes; a test for CLOSE-while-closed and for a controlled mount. The 1.6.0 docs (controlled-dialog.md) describe the current echo without counts.

findings.groupTitle: Escape in a dialog sends CLOSE twice, from the keyboard hook and from the dialog's own handler
findings.claim: react/hooks/use-keyboard.ts:53-55 with react/dialog.tsx:60-66: both handlers react to Escape and each sends CLOSE, so the machine runs two CLOSE events and emits two openChange callbacks (probed at the machine level by the DOCS cluster's verifier; the React path read, not run). Harmless today only because CLOSE is idempotent on state.
findings.fix: One owner for Escape (the dialog handler when the dialog is present, the hook otherwise); a test counts one CLOSE per Escape.

findings.groupTitle: In the virtualized list every activeId change, hover included, scrolls the active row to the top instead of only as far as needed
findings.claim: react/list.tsx:86-102: the virtualized branch scrolls to the active row with the row aligned at the top on every activeId change; a hover that activates a row already in view jumps the list. Read by the DOCS cluster's worker (examples/virtualized.md and guide/virtualization.md were corrected to describe it), not reproduced.
findings.fix: Scroll only when the active row is outside the viewport, with 'nearest' alignment, and not for pointer-driven activation; a browser test in the docs render suite or e2e.

findings.groupTitle: AsyncItems may register each loaded item twice: through ITEMS_LOADED under item.id and again through the rendered Command.Item's generated id
findings.claim: react/async-items.tsx: the component sends ITEMS_LOADED with the loaded items and also renders a Command.Item per item, whose useRegisterItem registers it again under its own id, so a loaded item can appear twice in the registry and the filtered ids. Unverified: read only by the DOCS cluster, no probe.
findings.fix: A probe test that loads two items through AsyncItems and asserts the registry holds exactly two; if the double registration is real, the rendered items reuse the loaded ids (or AsyncItems stops sending ITEMS_LOADED).

findings.groupTitle: registry.differenceFrom has no caller in the shipped source
findings.claim: core/registry.ts:158 defines differenceFrom; `grep -rn differenceFrom packages/modern-cmdk/src tests` on 1.6/docs finds the definition and one call in tests/unit/registry.test.ts:127, nothing in the shipped code. Dead surface area that the de-bloat phase removes or that a consumer-facing need justifies.
findings.fix: Remove differenceFrom and its test, or find the caller the method was written for and wire it; decided in the 1.7.0 de-bloat triage.
findings.note: Deferred to 1.12.0 (G-52): CommandRegistry is public through CommandMachine.getRegistry() (machine.ts:43), so D33 applies: differenceFrom is tested in 1.x (C7 of the 1.7.0 plan lands the test) and deprecated at 1.12.0; its removal or wiring is that deprecation's work.

findings.groupTitle: The machine's JSDoc example shows `using machine` plus subscribe at the top level, a pattern that disposes before any scheduled send runs
findings.claim: core/machine.ts:53-57: the example pairs `using machine = createCommandMachine(...)` with subscribe and send at the top level of a block; `using` disposes at the end of the block and send() is scheduled, so a reader copying it sees no state change. The same pattern was corrected in the docs (DAE-27, RDG-38) on 1.6/docs; the JSDoc still teaches it.
findings.fix: The example subscribes, sends and disposes on teardown (or awaits the next frame inside an async block with `await using`).
findings.note: The core/machine.ts JSDoc example creates the machine with const, subscribes, sends, and on teardown calls unsubscribe() and machine[Symbol.dispose](); no top-level using.

findings.groupTitle: When filteredCount crosses the virtualization threshold the list swaps between two wrapper trees and React remounts every Command.Item, doubling the registrations at mount
findings.claim: react/list.tsx:166-176 renders the items under one of two wrapper trees depending on whether filteredCount is above 100; the swap changes the element tree above every Command.Item, so React unmounts and remounts them all: N UNREGISTER_ITEM then N REGISTER_ITEM, a second scheduler batch and a second refilter. The CI record benchmarks/browser/results/1.4.0-8362840.json shows sends_after_mount 20000 at N=10000 and 2000 at N=1000 (RA-78 recorded the number; the docs verifier traced it to the swap while checking examples/virtualized.md:10, which claimed one refilter for 10K registrations).
findings.fix: One wrapper tree whose virtualization toggles inside the same component (or a keyed outer element kept stable across the threshold) so items keep their identity; the browser bench's sends_after_mount drops to N and the 10K mount loses its second batch. Measured before and after with the browser bench; examples/virtualized.md then drops the remount sentence.

findings.groupTitle: Under React StrictMode the hook's cleanup disposes the machine and nulls its ref, but the re-run effect creates nothing: the subtree keeps the disposed machine until the root renders again, so input before that re-render is dropped
findings.claim: react/hooks/use-command-setup.ts:49-56: the machine is created by a factory during render and held in a ref; StrictMode's development double-invocation runs the effect cleanup (dispose, ref = null) and then the effect again, which creates nothing; the context still hands the disposed machine to the subtree until the next render of the root, when the factory makes a fresh one. Probe (the CE-115 verifier, 2026-11-08): <StrictMode><Command items={[apple, banana]}><Command.Input /></Command></StrictMode>, type "ap" before any re-render: the SEARCH_CHANGE goes to the disposed machine and is dropped; the new machine starts with search "" and the input reads "". With <Command.Item> children the re-render happens during mount, which is why the StrictMode tests pass. The comment at :50-51 ("nulls the ref so Strict Mode remount creates a fresh machine") was false; 1.6.0 makes it true and names this row.
findings.fix: Hold the machine in state: the effect body creates a new machine when the held one is disposed and sets it into state, the cleanup disposes; a StrictMode test types before any re-render and asserts the query reaches a live machine. Development-only behaviour (StrictMode double-invocation), filed for 1.7.0 with the react size budget (90 B of headroom at 1.6.0) in view.

findings.groupTitle: BENCH's R4 allow-list test assumed unguarded scroll-driven properties; RA-77's @supports guard made three Biome allow entries dead and the pre-push unit gate went red
findings.claim: 1.6/bench (branched at ff2745c, before the CSS landing) added scroll-timeline, animation-timeline and animation-range to the useBaseline allowProperties list (5c08a99) and pinned each with 'R4: the allowed property %s is used by styles.css and reported once its allow entry is removed'. The CSS cluster's RA-77 (575be27) wrapped those properties in `@supports (animation-timeline: scroll())`, and Biome 2.6.6's suspicious/useBaseline does not report a property inside a matching @supports guard, so on the merged tree the three entries were dead and the three tests failed in the pre-push unit gate of the first push (3 failed of 2137). `git merge-tree` reported the branches clean: the coupling is semantic, not textual.
findings.fix: The three entries removed; the allow list keeps clip and user-select, both still reported when removed. Lesson for the landing procedure: a branch whose tests pin another cluster's file (here styles.css through the Biome config) is re-run on the merged tree before the push, not only probed with merge-tree; the pre-push gate (D88's companion) is the backstop that fired.
findings.note: The three dead allowProperties entries (scroll-timeline, animation-timeline, animation-range) removed; biome lint on styles.css stays clean because RA-77's @supports guard already keeps useBaseline from reporting them; the R4 allow-list test now runs over clip and user-select (73 passed). Caught by the pre-push unit gate of the first BENCH push (3 failed of 2137), not by the textual merge-tree probe.

findings.groupTitle: The bench compare computes sameMachine but its WARN/FAIL verdicts and exit codes ignore a CPU mismatch, so the ubuntu-26.04 pool's CPU gap alone can fail the Benchmarks job
findings.claim: compare-baseline.ts derives `sameMachine` from the baseline's environment.cpu and this machine's CPU (:380-383) and prints a cross-machine note (:430-434), but the per-row WARN/FAIL verdicts and the exit codes (:469-470: FAIL exits 2, WARN exits 1) apply the 5 %/15 % thresholds regardless. The ubuntu-26.04 pool handed out four CPU models on 2026-11-08 (AMD EPYC 7763, Intel Xeon Platinum 8573C, AMD EPYC 9V45, AMD EPYC 9V74). CI run 42461435971 (98b8949) ran the Benchmarks job on an EPYC 9V45 against benchmarks/baseline.json recorded four minutes earlier from run 42460937098 (201f701) on an EPYC 7763: search:ts-scorer-10k −48.5 %, stateUpdate:searchChange −51.1 %, stateUpdate:navigate −37.9 % (below floor), with no code change between the two runs. The inverse assignment, a 7763 run against a baseline recorded on a 9V45, reads about +90 % and fails the job (exit 2) for no code reason. The baseline committed at 98b8949 is a 7763 record, the slowest CPU the pool has shown, which is why both runs passed; D97 holds that line until the instrument is fixed.
findings.fix: Per-CPU baselines: benchmarks/baseline.json keeps one record per environment.cpu model; `pnpm bench:record` adds or replaces the record for the history file's CPU and refuses nothing else; `pnpm bench:compare` picks the record for this machine's CPU model and, when there is none, prints INFO 'no baseline for <cpu>' for every row, exits 0 and still writes the results artifact so the next record can add that CPU; the regression thresholds apply only to same-CPU comparisons. Tests: bench-compare-rules (same CPU: unchanged verdicts; other CPU with no record: INFO and exit 0; other CPU with a record: compared against that record), bench-record (adds a second CPU record, replaces the same CPU's). Docs: ci.yml's Benchmarks comments, CONTRIBUTING.md's bench section, apps/docs/benchmarks.md, benchmarks/README if present. Until then (D97): re-record only from an EPYC 7763 run; read cross-CPU numbers with both CPUs named.
findings.note: FIXED at d6aafd0 (1.7.0 C7a, 1.7/c7a): benchmarks/baseline.json is schemaVersion 2 with one record per CPU model under records[environment.cpu] and global regressionThresholds (5 % warn, 15 % fail, 0.01 ms floor, unchanged); the AMD EPYC 7763 record carries the previous file's numbers and meta byte-for-byte (verified by deep-equal and by re-recording the committed history file to an identical baseline). bench:compare applies WARN/FAIL only to the record whose key equals the run's CPU; a CPU without a record prints one INFO table per record naming both CPUs on every row and exits 0; exit codes 2/1/0 are otherwise unchanged; the results JSON (schema 2, 6882b59) carries comparedTo {record, cpu, node} and informational per-record deltas. bench:record writes only the record of the history file's environment.cpu and refuses a file without one (exit 2, nothing written). Tests: 'TEB-103: thresholds apply within one CPU model', 'TEB-103: a run on a CPU without a baseline record exits 0 with an informational table', 'TEB-103: bench:record writes only the record of the history file's CPU', 'TEB-103: a history file without environment.cpu is refused, nothing written'. Opus-verifier: four mutations each red on its test; a live run on the host (Intel Core Ultra 9 290HX Plus) INFO, exit 0. The act guard lands in 572d2a4, a46a6c5 and 8492273 (tests/act-guard.ts: a React act warning fails the test, recorded at call time so a silenced console.error cannot hide it; tests/unit/act-guard-usage.test.ts keeps swallowing spies out of tests/). 6882b59 brings every quoted benchmark figure in CONTRIBUTING.md, ARCHITECTURE.md, apps/docs/benchmarks.md, apps/docs/guide/wasm-search.md, ci.yml and compare-baseline.ts to the committed 7763 record (201f701, 2026-11-08). D97's interim clause ends here: every later record is written by the orchestrator through pnpm bench:record from a fully green run (D93).

findings.at: .github/workflows/ci.yml:404-417 (Links: lycheeverse/lychee-action v2.9.0 fetches lychee v0.24.2 from github.com/lycheeverse/lychee/releases/download with one `curl -sfLO`) and :661-669 (Package integrity: anchore/sbom-action v0.24.3 installs syft v1.57.0 through its installer, which fetches syft_1.57.0_checksums.txt from github.com/anchore/syft/releases/download once) at 36ad510
findings.groupTitle: The Links and Package integrity jobs download lychee and syft from GitHub's release-asset host without a retry, so a transient 504 of a host the repository does not control turns the run red
findings.claim: Both jobs fetch a third-party binary from github.com/<owner>/<repo>/releases/download before any repository code runs, and neither download retries. On 2026-11-08 run 42464306876 (a8c6bab, release/1.7.0) went red on one of them in all five attempts: attempt 1 both (the lychee tarball, curl exit 22; the syft checksums file, HTTP 504), attempts 2 to 4 the syft checksums file (504 each time, including after three consecutive 200 probes from the host), attempt 5 (a whole-run rerun) the lychee tarball (curl 22) while syft downloaded. The host fetched both assets with 200 throughout and the fresh runs 42465924038 (1488baf) and 42467217029 (2fc45fc) passed both jobs. Nothing in the tree is implicated; the owner's standard is green runs only.
findings.fix: Make both downloads retry and verify. Fetch each binary in a repository step with a retrying client (`curl --retry 8 --retry-all-errors --retry-delay 5 -fL`, or `gh release download`, which retries through the API) and check it against the release's published checksum, keeping lychee v0.24.2 and syft v1.57.0 pinned by version and digest, then hand the installed binary to the action or run the tool directly: read the pinned action.yml of lycheeverse/lychee-action v2.9.0 and anchore/sbom-action v0.24.3 for an input or a path that uses an already-installed binary before replacing an action by a direct invocation; never retry the whole job. The SBOM artifact and the link report keep their shape. Proof: a green run whose Links and Package integrity steps show the retrying fetch (SEC-72: a CI change counts only once green on GitHub); the matrix entry is a `gate` naming the two jobs.
findings.note: FIXED at 46b82d9..97750fb (1.7.0, 1.7/ci): a local composite action .github/actions/install-release-binary fetches a GitHub release asset with up to eight attempts (gh release download first, then curl through the API asset route (the asset id from /releases/tags/<tag>, Accept: application/octet-stream), then the direct release host, all with --retry-all-errors and connect and total timeouts; on 2026-11-08 the direct host answered 504 for over an hour while the API route served the same bytes at once), checks it against a sha256 pinned in the workflow next to the version, and installs the single binary either on GITHUB_PATH or into the runner tool cache with its .complete marker. Links: lychee v0.24.2 (lycheeverse/lychee-action dropped, its download had no retry and no checksum) installed on PATH and run with the flags the action's entrypoint used (--mode task --format markdown --output) plus the repository's config, excludes and file list; the report reaches the console and the job summary on success and on failure (|| status=$?, since GitHub runs bash -e), and a Total | 0 row fails the step. Package integrity: syft v1.57.0 seeded into $RUNNER_TOOL_CACHE/syft/1.57.0/x64 before anchore/sbom-action v0.24.3, whose getSyftCommand calls @actions/tool-cache find('syft', 'v1.57.0') before downloading, so the action skips install.sh and its un-retried checksums fetch; the sbom-action step itself is unchanged from 36ad510. release.yml: the same seeding step precedes the SBOM sites of first-publish-attest and attest (inline, since those jobs check out nothing, D62). Tests: 'tests/unit/release-workflow.test.ts::SEC-73: the seeded syft version and digest agree across ci.yml and release.yml' (release-workflow.test.ts; keeps the three digests, five syft-version lines and the seed tags and paths in step) and 'tests/unit/ci-workflow.test.ts::SEC-73: the Links step keeps lychee's report when lychee fails' (ci-workflow.test.ts). Verified by an opus-verifier in WSL under GitHub's exact bash -eo pipefail invocation: both install modes, wrong digest, wrong archive path, non-x86_64 and eight failed attempts all fail as intended; the live github.com release-asset host answered 504 three times in a row while the API route answered 302. Proof per SEC-72: the green run of the push that carries this landing.

findings.at: packages/modern-cmdk/src/core/utils/env.ts:17-23 and packages/modern-cmdk/src/react/hooks/use-devtools.ts:13-19 at b764df5; packages/modern-cmdk/src/react/hooks/use-command-setup.ts:18-24 on 1.7/c1 at f19ab96
findings.groupTitle: The isDev IIFEs survive minification with NODE_ENV defined, so production bundles carry the development-only code they guard
findings.claim: Each isDev flag is an IIFE (try { return process.env.NODE_ENV !== 'production' } catch { return false }) whose comment promises that consumer bundlers fold the guarded branches away. They do not: with process.env.NODE_ENV defined as "production" the IIFE minifies to (()=>{try{return!1}catch{return!1}})() and rolldown keeps it and every branch behind it, so the five size-limit rows measure byte-identical with and without the define (opus-verifier, 2026-11-08, on 1.7/c1 f19ab96 through a scratch modifyRolldownConfig; size-limit 14.3.0 itself defines no NODE_ENV). Production bundles of every 1.x release therefore carry core/search's window warning, the devtools hook body and, on 1.7/c1, the init-only prop warnings (230 to 256 B gzip per React row).
findings.fix: D105: the guard is the inline expression typeof process !== 'undefined' && process.env.NODE_ENV !== 'production' at each site (the typeof keeps a define-less browser import from throwing; the inline comparison folds under a define), in core/utils/env.ts, react/hooks/use-devtools.ts and react/hooks/use-command-setup.ts; the comments say what the code does. Proof: a build with the define contains none of the warning strings and the size-limit rows (which measure production per D105) drop by the guarded code's size; a test greps the built dist of a production-defined build for the warning strings.
